fragments.body:
Chix Cafe has a menu, but nobody looks at it. There is always a daily special. Everyone orders the daily special. And yet — ask anyone leaving the cafe to describe what they ate, and they go quiet in the same particular way, like they're reading something just past your shoulder.

"It was the special," they say. It is always the special. It has never once been anything else, and nobody has ever complained, which in Blind Eye is the highest praise a kitchen can earn.
fragments.thread: Lewis Ledbetter takes the corner booth every morning at seven. Watch what he does with the sugar packets.
fragments.title: The daily special

fragments.body:
Every spring, Lewis Ledbetter dyes baby chicks blue and sells them outside the cafe for two dollars each. The sign says BLUE CHIX $2.00, and the spelling has been argued about for a decade. The chicks are genuinely, vividly blue. By midsummer they are white again, and nobody mentions the blue period, the way you don't mention a friend's brief unhappy marriage.

Lewis says the dye recipe came from his grandmother. His grandmother, when asked, says she got it from a traveling man. The traveling man is never described the same way twice.
fragments.thread: Alvin Dupé bought twelve one spring. Ask him what happened to them. Actually — don't.
fragments.title: Blue chicks, $2.00

name: Chix Cafe
tagline: Home of the daily special and the blue chicks.
